title: Media Trust Is Built Two Ways, Not One
hook: Most fixes for distrust in the press ask journalists to try harder. Research on Black communities in Minneapolis found the overlooked half is whether the community engages back.
key_points: Trust in journalism has fallen sharply over the past decade, and further in communities with a history of being misrepresented.
Mainstream outlets have overrepresented Black people in crime coverage and misframed protest and health reporting.
Study basis: a 2022 survey of 100+ Black community members in Minneapolis–Saint Paul plus interviews with 17 trusted journalists.
Diligence — showing up in a community continuously, beyond what the assignment requires.
Deference — respecting boundaries and cultural norms, letting people shape their own story.
The author's core claim: trust is bidirectional; communities must also engage, forgive, and voice concern.
content_html: Trust in journalism has dropped sharply over the past decade, and the standard prescriptions all point one way: journalists should be more accurate, more transparent, more accountable. Danielle K. Brown, a journalism professor at Michigan State University, argues in The Conversation that this framing quietly misses half the problem. Drawing on a 2022 study of more than 100 Black community members in Minneapolis–Saint Paul — conducted after George Floyd's murder — alongside interviews with 17 journalists those communities named as trusted, she makes the case that trust is something two parties build, not something a newsroom delivers.
extra_html:
The starting point is that distrust is often earned. Brown notes the documented pattern of mainstream media overrepresenting Black people in crime coverage and misrepresenting them in protest, crime, and health reporting, which is why these communities have a long history of turning away from mainstream journalism. Against that backdrop, the journalists who did earn trust shared two practices. The first is diligence: spending extended time in the community, staying for the whole event rather than the quotable part, being a regular presence at local spaces beyond what an assignment demands. The second is deference: respecting boundaries, honoring cultural norms, and what she calls intentional humility — arriving without a predetermined narrative and letting people retain authorship of their own story.

Brown's sharpest point is the other direction. The most overlooked piece, she writes, is a community's own willingness to engage — to offer perspectives, to give feedback both critical and affirming, to share knowledge rather than withhold it. It takes communities willing to engage, forgive, and voice concern. That reframing matters for civic life generally: a press that functions as a check on power depends on a public that stays in contact with it, which makes media trust a shared civic responsibility rather than a service the industry either provides or fails to.

source.name: The Conversation
authors: Danielle K. Brown, Professor of Journalism, Michigan State University

flashcards.prompt: What are the two journalist practices the study identifies as trust-building?

choices.text: Diligence — sustained presence in the community — and deference to its boundaries and norms
Speed of publication and volume of coverage
Strict neutrality and refusing all community contact
Anonymous sourcing and aggressive confrontation of officials

flashcards.explanation_html: Diligence means showing up continuously, past what the job requires; deference means intentional humility — letting community members retain autonomy over how their story is told.

flashcards.prompt: Why does distrust of the press run deeper in some communities than others?
flashcards.back_html: Because of accumulated, documented harm — mainstream media has overrepresented Black people in crime coverage and misframed protest and health reporting, giving those communities reason to turn away.

flashcards.prompt: What does the author call the most overlooked ingredient in media trust?

choices.text: A community's own willingness to engage with journalists

flashcards.explanation_html: The argument is that trust is bidirectional: journalists must earn it, but communities have to supply perspectives, give critical and affirming feedback, and be willing to engage.
